summary: The exact bundle (org-wide repo catalogue plus PR policy gate with exceptions) is not owned by anyone yet, but each piece is: GitHub controls the merge gate and can bundle org policies, SCA vendors already block banned components/versions on PRs, secret scanners and free tools (Danger, Probot, OPA) cover the rest. Viable only if the catalogue and governance layer is clearly deeper than platform settings.

objections.objection: Most dangerous competitor is GitHub itself: it owns the pull-request merge gate, branch protection and required checks, and builds app/checks APIs precisely so it can absorb popular third-party use cases. Organisation-level rules, dependency alerts and secret detection are natural roadmap items; the concept's own risk list names this. A product whose enforcement point is a platform API it does not control can be commoditised in one release.

Three of the four example policies (banned components, approved versions, secrets) are already sold by entrenched SCA and secret-scanning vendors (Snyk, Black Duck, WhiteSource-type SCA policy engines, plus free secret scanners) that already sit on the PR and have security budget. The concept frames Snyk as 'only vulnerable dependencies', which understates SCA license/version policy features, leaving Tamarind with the residual 'required files / best practice' rules, which are low value.

Free do-it-yourself substitutes are strong for a platform team at 50-500 engineers: Danger for PR rules, Probot apps for org-wide GitHub automation, and Open Policy Agent for centrally managed policy-as-code. Platform teams are the users who define policies and are exactly the people inclined to script this themselves, which caps price at $15/dev.

Code-quality and DevSecOps suites (SonarQube quality gates, Code Climate, GitLab with push rules and built-in security) can extend into cross-repo policy dashboards; the differentiation 'policy rather than metrics' is a positioning statement, not a capability gap they cannot close.
GitHub-only scope in v1 excludes GitLab/Bitbucket shops and ties the whole TAM to one platform's goodwill and API terms.

strongest_point: No incumbent yet offers a metadata-only, organisation-wide catalogue of repos, teams and components joined to PR policy enforcement with exceptions; that governance layer is a genuine white space.
what_would_change_my_mind: Design partners who already pay for an SCA tool still list cross-repo catalogue/governance as unmet
At least 3 of 6 design partners choose a paid Tamarind pilot over scripting Danger/Probot/OPA themselves
Most enforced policies are ones SCA and secret scanners don't cover (ownership, service metadata, required runbooks)
